items.prompt: Which three parts make up the basic structure of a speech?

options.label: Opening joke, statistics, closing quote
Introduction, body, conclusion
Problem, delay, solution
Question, answer, summary

rubric: A speech basically has an introduction, body and conclusion.
Other options list techniques or story pieces, not the core structure.

items.prompt: What is the term for the people who listen to your talk?

options.label: Delegate
Moderator
Respondent
Audience

rubric: The listeners are the audience.
A moderator runs the session; the other terms refer to specific roles.

items.prompt: What is the main purpose of a speech introduction?

options.label: To gain attention and tell listeners what the talk is about
To thank everyone who helped prepare the talk
To answer all questions before they are asked
To list every detail the audience should remember

rubric: Introductions capture attention and preview the topic.
Listing details or answering questions belongs in the body or Q&A.

items.prompt: What does the term 'eye contact' mean in public speaking?

options.label: Staring at one person for the whole talk
Reading your notes without looking up
Looking at the back wall above everyone
Looking at different audience members while speaking

rubric: Eye contact means looking at various listeners to connect.
Staring or avoiding gaze fails to engage the whole audience.

items.prompt: What is a 'pause' in speaking?

options.label: A deliberate short silence between ideas
A slower speaking speed throughout
A mistake where you forget your words
A filler sound such as 'um'

rubric: A pause is a deliberate silence used for emphasis or clarity.
Fillers and forgetting are not deliberate pauses.

items.prompt: Which of these are elements of vocal delivery? Select all that apply.

options.label: Slide colour
Pace
Room temperature
Volume

rubric: Volume and pace are voice qualities.
Slide colour and room temperature are not about the voice.

items.prompt: Maria is preparing a five-minute talk. Her teacher says: 'Start with a hook, then give your main points, then end with a summary.' Which part of the speech is the 'hook' meant to be?

options.label: The question-and-answer session
The introduction
The main body
The conclusion

rubric: A hook opens the talk to grab attention in the introduction.
The other parts come later in the speech.

items.prompt: Why is it useful to rehearse a speech aloud before giving it?

options.label: It lets you memorise every word exactly
It shows you can skip preparing notes
It helps you check timing and spot awkward phrases
It guarantees you will never feel nervous

rubric: Rehearsing aloud reveals timing and wording issues.
It reduces but does not eliminate nerves, and word-perfect memorising is not the goal.

items.prompt: Why should a speaker adapt the language to the audience?

options.label: So the speaker needs fewer examples
So listeners can follow and relate to the message
So the talk can be made as short as possible
So the speaker can show off specialist words

rubric: Adapting language helps the audience understand.
The other choices misstate the aim of adaptation.

items.prompt: A speaker's hands shake before a talk. Which explanation of this is most accurate?

options.label: It will get worse if the speaker breathes slowly
It proves the speaker is unprepared
It means the talk should be cancelled
It is a normal body response to nerves that can be managed

rubric: Shaking is a common stress response and manageable.
Slow breathing calms nerves rather than worsening them.

items.prompt: Which example shows open body language?

options.label: Holding the lectern tightly and leaning on it
Crossing arms and looking at the floor
Turning to the screen and reading from it
Standing upright with relaxed arms and facing the audience

rubric: Upright, relaxed posture facing listeners looks open.
The others show closed or disengaged habits.

items.prompt: What is the best way to describe the purpose of a conclusion?

options.label: To apologise for anything that went wrong
To add several new points not yet covered
To reinforce the main message and leave a lasting finish
To pause until someone starts clapping

rubric: A conclusion reinforces the key message.
New points or apologies weaken the ending.

items.prompt: Which statements correctly explain why speakers use signposting phrases such as 'first' and 'next'? Select all that apply.

options.label: They replace the need for a conclusion
They help listeners follow the structure
They make the speech sound longer without content
They show when the speaker moves to a new point

rubric: Signposts guide listeners and mark transitions.
They do not replace conclusions or merely add length.

items.prompt: Tom gives a talk to classmates but speaks very fast and never pauses. Afterwards, listeners say they could not keep up. What is the most likely reason for this?

options.label: The talk had too few points
His slides were printed in colour
The audience was not interested in the topic
Fast speech with no pauses leaves listeners no time to process ideas

rubric: Pace without pauses overloads listeners.
The other reasons do not explain the feedback.

items.prompt: A speaker says, "Now that we've covered the cost, let's turn to the risks." What is the main purpose of this kind of signpost?

options.label: It replaces the need for an introduction that previews the talk's main points
It gives the speaker a few seconds to recall the next point without leaving silence
It tells listeners where they are in the talk so they can follow its structure
It shows the audience that the speaker has finished the most important material

rubric: Signposts orient listeners within the structure of the talk.
Distractors treat signposts as a memory aid or a substitute for a preview, which misses their purpose for the audience.

items.prompt: Why do effective speakers often pause briefly after a key statement?

options.label: It lets the speaker check their notes, which is why audiences expect pauses at that point
It fills time when a talk is shorter than planned without changing how clear it is
It lowers the speaker's heart rate, which is the only benefit and has no effect on listeners
It gives listeners time to absorb the point and signals that the point matters

rubric: A pause lets the audience process the idea and adds emphasis.
Distractors see pauses as only a benefit to the speaker or as filler.

items.prompt: Which of these openings is best classified as an attention-grabbing hook?

options.label: "Sorry, I'm not very prepared, so please bear with me."
"First I'll read out the agenda, and then we'll begin."
"Thank you all for coming today; I'm glad to see so many of you."
"Every day, about 1 in 3 meals we buy ends up in the bin."

rubric: A surprising, relevant statistic draws attention and raises curiosity.
Thanks, apologies and agenda reading are common openings but do not hook the audience.

items.prompt: Why should a speaker find out about the audience before writing the talk?

options.label: A speaker who knows the audience no longer needs to rehearse or structure the talk
Audiences prefer talks that are shorter whenever they know less about the subject matter
Knowing the audience lets the speaker reuse one script for every group with only small edits
The same content needs different vocabulary, examples and depth depending on what listeners know and need

rubric: Audience knowledge guides choices of language, examples and depth.
Distractors claim one script fits all or that analysis replaces preparation.

items.prompt: A speaker tells herself, "I'm excited," rather than "I'm terrified," before going on stage. Why can this reframing help?

options.label: Both feelings involve similar arousal, so calling it energy lets her use it rather than fight it
It convinces the audience that she is not nervous, whatever she is actually feeling
It shows that preparation is unnecessary, because adrenaline improves memory on its own
It removes the physical symptoms of nerves entirely, so she feels calm before starting

rubric: Nerves and excitement share physical arousal, so relabelling it channels it into energy.
Distractors suggest the reframing deletes symptoms or replaces preparation.

items.prompt: Which behaviours help body language support a speaker's message? Select all that apply.

options.label: Gestures that match the points being made
Standing with hands gripped behind the back to stay still
Pacing constantly to burn off nervous energy
Eye contact shared with different people across the room
Facing the screen while explaining each slide

rubric: Purposeful gestures and varied eye contact reinforce the message and build connection.
Constant pacing, rigid posture and facing the screen distract or disconnect from the audience.

items.prompt: A new employee fills each slide with full paragraphs and reads them aloud word for word. After a few minutes, most of the audience is looking at their phones. Which explanation best accounts for the loss of attention?

options.label: Audiences dislike slides in any form, so any visuals cause attention to fall quickly
Listeners read faster than the speaker talks, so the speaker adds little and attention drifts
Reading aloud makes the voice too quiet, which is the only real cause of disengagement
Long paragraphs are too hard for any audience to understand, even when read slowly

rubric: When the speaker only repeats on-screen text, listeners read ahead and have no reason to listen.
Distractors blame slides in general, volume or comprehension difficulty instead of redundancy.

items.prompt: You have exactly 5 minutes for a talk with an opening, three main points and a close. Which plan uses the full five minutes?

options.label: Opening 30 seconds, three points of 1 min 20 seconds each, close 30 seconds
Opening 15 seconds, three points of 2 minutes each, close 15 seconds
Opening 1 min, three points of 2 minutes each, close 1 min
Opening 1 min, three points of 1 min each, close 30 seconds

rubric: 30s + 3 x 80s + 30s = 5 minutes.
The other plans total 4.5, 6.5 and 8 minutes, so they under-run or overrun.

items.prompt: A slide holds a 60-word paragraph about Q3 sales growth. Which revision best applies the rule that slides support rather than repeat the speaker?

options.label: Keep the paragraph and read it slowly so that all the detail reaches the audience
Show the headline "Sales grew 12% in Q3" with one simple chart, and say the detail aloud
Print the paragraph on the slide in bold so the main numbers are all highlighted
Shrink the font so the paragraph fits, then bullet every sentence of it

rubric: A headline and one visual with spoken detail lets the slide support the talk.
Other options keep dense text, which listeners read instead of listening.

items.prompt: You are giving a talk by video call and want to feel connected to the audience. Where should you mainly look when making your key points?

options.label: At the faces on the screen throughout, so you can read every reaction continuously
At the camera lens, glancing at the screen only to check slides or reactions
At your own video thumbnail, so that you can keep monitoring your posture
At notes placed beside the screen, so that you never lose your place in the talk

rubric: Looking at the lens appears as eye contact to viewers.
Looking at faces, notes or your own image makes you appear to look away.

items.prompt: During Q&A someone asks a relevant question you cannot answer. What is the best response?

options.label: Tell the person the question is off-topic and ask them to leave it for later
Say you don't know, offer to find out and follow up, then move to the next question
Redirect to a related strength of yours so that you avoid admitting any gap
Give a confident-sounding guess so that the audience keeps trusting your expertise

rubric: Honesty plus a follow-up keeps credibility.
Guessing, dodging or dismissing a valid question damages trust.

items.prompt: You are speaking to new customers with no technical background. Which version of this sentence should you use? Original: "Our API uses asynchronous, non-blocking I/O for throughput."

options.label: "Our system handles many requests at once, so pages load quickly for you."
"Our API's throughput is improved by asynchronous I/O, as engineers know well."
"Our API handles asynchronous requests, which means it is non-blocking."
"Our API uses non-blocking I/O, which is a standard technique for throughput."

rubric: Plain language that links to a customer benefit suits a non-technical audience.
The other versions keep jargon or only restate it.

items.prompt: You give a 10-minute talk tomorrow. Which preparation steps are most useful tonight? Select all that apply.

options.label: Skip rehearsal so that you sound spontaneous
Add extra material in case you finish early
Memorise the script word for word
Write your main message as one clear sentence
Rehearse aloud with a timer

rubric: Timed rehearsal checks length and delivery; a one-sentence message focuses the content.
Memorising word for word, padding and skipping rehearsal raise the risk of freezing, overrunning or rambling.

items.prompt: You have a 12-minute slot with four sections. At minute 9 you have finished only two sections, and the last two were planned at 3 minutes each. You want to finish on time and still close well. What should you do?

options.label: Speak faster so that both remaining sections are covered at the planned level of detail
Ask the audience for extra time and continue as planned if nobody objects
Skip the conclusion and use the remaining time to cover both sections in full
Condense sections three and four to the key point of each, then give your planned close

rubric: Trimming the remaining sections to their essentials keeps both the content and the close within time.
Rushing, dropping the conclusion or overrunning each harm clarity or disrespect the time limit.

items.prompt: You have 10 minutes to present a quarterly sales review to senior executives who have said they will decide on budget right after. Which opening applies the principle of leading with the audience's need?

options.label: State the headline result and the budget decision you need, then give supporting data
Open with a joke about quarterly reviews to relax the room before the results
Walk through each month in order so the executives can follow how you reached it
Begin with the company history so the executives share your context before the data

rubric: Decision-makers with limited time need the conclusion and request first, then support.
Chronological or background openings delay the point and suit audiences who need context, not decisions.

items.prompt: You must deliver a 15-minute talk with three main points. You rehearse and it runs 19 minutes. Which adjustment best applies sound time management?

options.label: Remove the third main point entirely and spend the saved time on the first two
Speak faster throughout so the full content still fits into fifteen minutes
Drop the conclusion, since the audience already heard the main points earlier
Cut or condense supporting detail within each point, keeping all three main points

rubric: Trimming supporting detail preserves structure and pacing.
Speeding up hurts clarity; dropping the conclusion or a whole point damages the talk's structure.

items.prompt: Your hands shake before a talk begins and your breathing is shallow. You have two minutes. Which action best applies a nerve-management technique?

options.label: Drink a large coffee so you feel more alert and energetic when you begin speaking
Take slow breaths with a longer exhale, then plant your feet and start with your rehearsed first line
Tell yourself firmly to stop being nervous so the shaking goes away before you start
Reread all your notes quickly to make sure you have not forgotten anything

rubric: Slow exhale breathing lowers arousal and a rehearsed opening gives a stable start.
Caffeine increases shakiness; suppressing nerves by command or last-minute cramming raises anxiety.

items.prompt: You are presenting a technical process to a mixed audience on a video call. You want to keep remote attendees engaged. Which technique should you apply?

options.label: Ask a short poll or chat question every few minutes and respond to the answers aloud
Read the slides word for word so remote attendees do not miss any content
Keep your camera off so the slides are the only thing people have to watch
Save all questions for the end so nothing interrupts the flow of the talk

rubric: Regular interaction counters virtual disengagement.
Hiding, deferring all questions, or reading slides reduce engagement.

items.prompt: You are asked to explain a new expense policy to 40 new hires with no finance background. Which choice best applies adapting your message to the audience?

options.label: Replace jargon with plain terms and give one worked example of a typical expense claim
Provide the full policy document and summarise only the sections you consider hard
Use the exact policy wording so nothing is misstated, and define terms afterwards
Cover the policy's history first so new hires understand why each rule exists

rubric: Plain language plus a concrete example fits novices.
Policy wording, history, or document dumps do not adapt content to the audience's level.

items.prompt: You are preparing a 5-minute persuasive talk asking your team to adopt a new meeting schedule. Which steps apply sound structuring practice? Select all that apply.

options.label: State your recommendation clearly and repeat it in the closing
Open with a problem the team already feels about current meetings
End with a new topic after your request to keep the audience curious
Add as many side topics as possible to show how much you researched
Give three or four reasons, ordered from strongest to supporting

rubric: Opening with a felt problem, a clear ask repeated at the end, and a focused set of reasons structure persuasion.
Side topics and new material after the ask dilute the message.

items.prompt: You will give a 20-minute talk in a large hall with a microphone clipped to your collar. You tend to walk constantly while speaking and look at your slides. A colleague says it distracts people. Which change best applies good delivery technique?

options.label: Pause your movement at key points, face the audience and glance at slides only briefly
Keep walking but speed up so the movement looks more energetic and purposeful
Stand behind the lectern for the whole talk and read from the slides to avoid pacing
Look at one friendly person in the front row for the whole talk to feel more comfortable

rubric: Purposeful movement and facing the audience keep attention and connection.
Hiding, speeding up, or fixing on one person do not fix the distraction or engage the room.

items.prompt: After a talk, listeners can recall your examples but not your main recommendation. Which diagnosis best explains this?

options.label: Your slides had too much white space, which pulled attention away from the recommendation
Your voice was too loud, which made the examples more memorable than the point
The recommendation was not signposted or repeated, so the examples overshadowed it
You used too few examples, so there was nothing to anchor the recommendation

rubric: Without signposting and repetition, vivid examples can overshadow the main point.
Loudness, too few examples, or white space do not explain recall of examples over the message.

items.prompt: A speaker's delivery of a rehearsed talk sounds flat. Recording shows steady pace, same pitch, and no pauses, while the content is strong. Which is the most likely cause?

options.label: The speaker is reciting memorised wording rather than thinking through the ideas as they speak
The speaker is using too many gestures, which flattens the voice automatically
The content is too complex, so the audience cannot show any interest in it
The speaker has chosen the wrong topic for the audience's interests

rubric: Monotone, steady pacing with no pauses typically signals recitation of memorised text.
Content complexity, topic choice, and gestures do not explain a flat vocal pattern.

items.prompt: In a Q&A, a speaker answers a hostile question with a long defensive reply and loses the room. Which breakdown of the exchange best identifies the error?

options.label: The speaker responded to the tone instead of restating and answering the underlying question briefly
The speaker answered too briefly, which showed a lack of knowledge on the subject
The speaker gave a reply that was too calm, which made the questioner more hostile
The speaker should have ignored the question and moved to a friendlier one immediately

rubric: Restating the real question and answering concisely defuses hostility.
Ignoring the question or blaming calm or brevity misreads the cause.

items.prompt: The same 10-minute talk got strong engagement with a local team in person but weak engagement on a video call with the same people. Which comparison best explains the difference?

options.label: The content was shorter online, so people had less time to engage
Online audiences are always less intelligent, so they need a simpler talk
In-person talks never need interaction, so the online version needed more slides
Online, the speaker lost audience cues and visual variety, so pacing and interaction did not adapt

rubric: Virtual settings reduce feedback cues, so the speaker must adapt pacing and add interaction.
The other options are false or irrelevant to the difference between settings.

items.prompt: A speaker's talk has an introduction, five main points, and a quick closing line. Listeners say they felt lost halfway. Which part of the structure most likely caused this?

options.label: The introduction was too short to provide any background for the talk
The points were all relevant, which made them harder to separate from one another
Five points with no signposts or summaries between them, which overloaded listeners' tracking
The closing line was too quick, which caused confusion earlier in the talk

rubric: Many points without signposts or recaps cause listeners to lose their place.
A short intro or closing does not explain mid-talk confusion, and relevance is not a problem.

items.prompt: A speaker reads dense bullet slides aloud and the audience seems restless. Which factors are plausible causes of the disengagement? Select all that apply.

options.label: Listeners read faster than the speaker talks, so the speech adds nothing
The slides give the audience no visual cue about which point matters most
The speaker's choice of a dark background caused the restlessness by itself
Using any slides at all makes every audience restless
Dense text splits attention between reading and listening

rubric: Reading ahead, split attention, and no emphasis cues all explain the effect.
Background colour alone or slides in general are not causes.

items.prompt: A manager delivers a 12-minute update to the board. She spends eight minutes on methodology and two on results, then runs out of time before her recommendation. Board members look impatient. Which analysis best identifies the root problem?

options.label: She included results, which are not needed by a board meeting about a decision
She should have had no recommendation, since boards prefer to draw conclusions themselves
She organised the talk around her process rather than the board's decision needs, so the key content came too late
She spoke too slowly, and the board would be satisfied if she simply had a faster voice

rubric: The structure followed her work rather than the audience's decision needs, pushing results and recommendation to the end.
Speed, including results, or omitting a recommendation misdiagnose the cause.

items.prompt: A speaker gives a 15-minute update to executives: 10 minutes of project history, then her recommendation in the last 3 minutes. In Q&A, most questions ask what she recommends. Which explanation fits best?

options.label: Fifteen minutes is too long for any update, so nothing could have been remembered by anyone at all
The recommendation came after so much background that the audience never identified it as the main point
The executives were too senior to follow any talk that included project history, however it was ordered
Her voice dropped in volume during the final three minutes, so the recommendation could not be heard

rubric: Burying the key message late means listeners did not know what to track; structure, not length or volume, is the cause.
Distractors blame audience seniority, volume or length without evidence in the situation.

items.prompt: A presenter walks through a dense results table at a fast, even pace with no pauses. Listeners later say they 'followed the words but lost the numbers.' Which diagnosis fits best?

options.label: The table font was too small to read, so enlarging it would have fixed the whole problem
Her pronunciation of the figures was unclear, so listeners could not catch the numbers she said
Her gestures competed with the numbers, so listeners watched her hands instead of listening to her
Dense new data needs processing time, and with no pauses or signposting listeners could not link numbers to meaning

rubric: Listeners could hear the words but had no time or cues to process the data; pacing and signposting address this.
Distractors name surface causes (diction, font, gestures) that the feedback does not point to.

items.prompt: A speaker puts full sentences on every slide and reads them aloud word for word. Feedback: 'I stopped listening after two slides.' Which mechanism most likely explains this?

options.label: Audiences distrust any speaker who glances at the screen, whatever the slides happen to contain at the time
Full sentences are too grammatical, and audiences prefer fragments because fragments sound more casual to them
Reading aloud makes any speaker's voice monotone by definition, and monotone delivery always ends attention
Listeners read faster than a speaker talks, so they finish early and the spoken words add nothing new

rubric: Redundant text and speech split attention and the audience is ahead of the speaker, so the talk adds nothing.
Distractors rely on absolute claims about monotone voices, grammar or screen glances.

items.prompt: A speaker's voice shakes and her pace races for the first minute, then she settles for the rest of the talk. Which cause and adjustment best fit this pattern?

options.label: Adrenaline peaks just before the start, so a memorised opening and a slow breath steady the first minute
The room was too warm, so presenting in a cooler room is the only way to prevent early shaking
She lacks topic knowledge, so more research would remove the shake from her opening minute next time
Her nerves last all talk, so she should avoid eye contact until the shaking has completely stopped

rubric: Symptoms that fade after the start point to an early adrenaline peak, which a rehearsed opening and breathing target.
Distractors ignore the pattern: knowledge gaps or constant nerves would not fade, and temperature is an unsupported cause.

items.prompt: A presenter finds that in virtual talks attention (cameras off, silent chat) falls around minute 10, while the same content holds attention in person. Which analysis best explains the difference?

options.label: Virtual platforms compress audio so voices lose emotional content, which makes listeners tune out by minute ten
Online audiences are simply weaker listeners, so the content should be simplified until they can follow it
Ten minutes is a hard biological limit, so in-person audiences must also stop listening without it showing
Online, visible audience cues vanish and other tabs are one click away, so attention needs planned resets

rubric: Without feedback cues and with easy distractions, virtual talks need deliberate interaction to reset attention.
Distractors blame audience ability, a fixed limit or audio compression, none of which explain the in-person contrast.

items.prompt: Which of the following features of a talk's structure would most likely cause listeners to lose the thread? Select all that apply.

options.label: Previewing three points at the start and then covering them in that order
Adding a tangent mid-section that is never connected back to the main argument
Introducing a third key term before the first two have been used in an example
Switching topics with no transition or signpost between sections
Briefly repeating the core message in the conclusion

rubric: Stacked terms, missing signposts and unconnected tangents all break the audience's mental map.
Previewing and repeating the core message are standard aids, not causes of confusion.

items.prompt: A consultant presents a cloud migration plan to a mixed room. Engineers nod during the architecture section, but the finance leads stop taking notes and one checks her phone. The consultant used terms like 'egress' and 'IaC' without defining them. What is the best analysis of what happened?

options.label: The engineers' nodding distracted the finance leads, so seating the two groups apart would have solved it
The architecture section was too short, so the finance leads had no time to form questions about it
The finance leads lacked the vocabulary to link the architecture to cost, so the talk was pitched at one segment
The finance leads are uninterested in technology, so no change to the talk would have kept them engaged

rubric: Undefined jargon cut one segment off from the content; the talk was not adapted to the mixed audience.
Distractors blame disinterest, section length or seating rather than the audience mismatch.

items.prompt: You have 5 minutes to open a budget-cut proposal to a skeptical board. Criteria: earn attention fast, avoid defensiveness, signal the ask. Which opening best meets these criteria?

options.label: Open with a long apology for the cuts to lower defensiveness, then list every line item of the proposal
Open with a joke about budgets to relax the room, then move to the history of the department's spending
Open with an agenda and credentials slide so skeptics trust your authority before you reach the ask
Open with the board's own stated goal, show how current spending blocks it, then name the decision you need

rubric: Starting from the board's goal earns attention, frames the cuts as serving them and signals the ask early.
Distractors delay the ask or invite defensiveness through humour, apology or credentials.

items.prompt: A 20-minute talk will be interrupted by questions. Criteria: recover quickly after interruptions, sound natural, cover the key points. Which preparation is best?

options.label: Read from a full script on the lectern, since interruptions then cost nothing and wording stays exact
Rehearse from a keyword outline with practised transitions, so you can resume anywhere and phrase naturally
Improvise from the title slide only, since interruptions make any prepared structure useless for the speaker
Memorise the full script so every sentence is exactly as planned and nothing is left to chance

rubric: An outline with practised transitions supports recovery and natural delivery while keeping the structure.
Memorising or reading from a script makes recovery and natural delivery hard; pure improvisation drops the key points.

items.prompt: A one-shot virtual keynote for 500 people centres on a live product demo. Criterion: mitigate first the risk that would make the whole talk worthless and cannot be fixed live. Which mitigation should come first?

options.label: Test several opening jokes with colleagues, since a weak opening is the largest threat to the talk
Rehearse hand gestures until they look polished, since awkward movement on camera would damage credibility
Prepare a recorded backup of the demo, ready to play if the live demo fails during the session
Commission a brand review of slide colours, since inconsistent design would undermine the message overall

rubric: Demo failure is the one risk that destroys the core message and cannot be fixed live, so a fallback comes first.
The other options address real but recoverable, lower-impact risks.

items.prompt: You have 3 minutes to show a board a 12-month sales chart. Criteria: they must grasp the trend and one implication, and detail should stay available. Which approach is best?

options.label: Show one simplified chart with the key change highlighted, say the implication, and put detail in a handout
Show the full 12-month table so the board can verify every number themselves during the talk
Read out all twelve monthly figures slowly so that nothing is misunderstood by anyone in the room
Show five charts in quick succession so the board sees that the analysis was thorough and complete

rubric: One highlighted chart with a stated implication fits the time and the aim; a handout keeps detail available.
Distractors overload the audience with tables, charts or spoken figures.

items.prompt: In Q&A a hostile attendee asks a question built on a false premise. Criteria: keep your credibility, avoid escalation, serve the rest of the audience. Which response is best?

options.label: Correct the premise with one fact, address the underlying concern, and offer to continue afterwards
Ignore the premise and answer a different, easier question so the exchange ends without any conflict
Tell the questioner they are wrong and ask them to move on, so the remaining audience stays on schedule
Accept the premise as stated to keep the peace, then adjust the rest of your talk to fit that premise

rubric: A brief factual correction plus answering the real concern protects credibility and avoids escalation.
Distractors escalate, concede a falsehood or dodge the question.

items.prompt: Your 30-minute slot is cut to 15 minutes. Criteria: keep the decision-critical content and preserve clarity. Which cuts are well justified? Select all that apply.

options.label: Cut a second case study that repeats the point of the first
Cut the recommendation, since the audience can read it in the follow-up email
Cut background the audience already knows from the pre-read
Speak twice as fast so all slides fit unchanged
Move optional detail slides to an appendix

rubric: Redundant, already-known and optional material can go without harming the decision or clarity.
Cutting the recommendation or doubling the pace sacrifices the decision-critical content or clarity.

items.prompt: Midway through a 10-minute pitch, the organiser signals that you have 3 minutes left, but 5 minutes of content remain, including your ask. Criteria: the ask must land, the audience keeps clarity, your credibility stays intact. What is the best move?

options.label: Drop the ask and finish the details, since the audience can request the recommendation later in writing
Skip the least critical points, mention the cut briefly, and give the ask and a clear close in time
Speed up and cover everything, since skipping any content would make you look unprepared to the audience
Stop and ask the organiser for extra time, since the ask needs the full five minutes to be understood

rubric: Prioritising the ask, trimming the least critical points and closing clearly meets all three criteria.
Distractors sacrifice clarity by rushing, credibility by demanding time, or the ask itself.

items.prompt: A speaker plans to memorise a 40-minute keynote word for word to control nerves, and a Q&A follows. Which critique best judges this plan against the criteria of resilience and natural delivery?

options.label: It is weak mainly because audiences notice memorised talks and dislike them, whatever the speaker's skill, so notes should be read.
It is fragile: one lapse breaks the chain, and recited text flattens delivery, so rehearsing a structure with flexible wording is sturdier.
It is sound, because exact wording removes decisions on stage and so lowers the cognitive load that causes most nerves.
It is weak only because 40 minutes is too long, since memorising anything under 15 minutes is reliably safe for any speaker.

rubric: Verbatim recall leaves no recovery path after a lapse and tends to sound recited; a memorised structure with flexible phrasing is more robust.
Distractors treat memorisation as risk-free, or swap in reading from notes or a simple length cutoff.

items.prompt: You must propose a pricing change to a sceptical audience that opposes it. Criteria: earn credibility in the first minute and avoid triggering defensiveness. Which opening is best?

options.label: Name a problem both sides already agree exists, then show the proposal as one response to it, so the audience reaches your logic with you.
Open with a vivid personal anecdote about your own career, so the audience warms to you before any contentious topic appears.
State the proposal and its headline benefit at once, so the audience knows your position and can weigh the evidence you give next.
Acknowledge that many will disagree and apologise in advance, so the audience sees humility and lowers its guard toward you.

rubric: Shared ground first builds credibility and delays the reflex to counter-argue.
Leading with the proposal triggers resistance; the anecdote is irrelevant to the criteria; pre-apologising weakens authority.

items.prompt: A 45-minute webinar for 200 attendees with cameras off must sustain attention with minimal technical risk. Which plan best meets both criteria?

options.label: Use breakout rooms every ten minutes, because small-group discussion is the strongest engagement tool in any virtual setting.
Embed a short chat prompt or poll every five to seven minutes, with a spoken fallback if the tool fails, then read out some answers.
Show a new animated slide every minute to give the eye constant change, since visual novelty holds attention best online.
Speak with high energy throughout and save all questions for the end, so the flow stays uninterrupted by technology glitches.

rubric: Frequent low-tech interaction with a fallback balances attention and risk.
Breakouts at 200 attendees add risk; energy alone does not create participation; constant animation distracts.

items.prompt: Ten minutes before a 10-minute investor pitch, you learn your slot is cut to 7 minutes. Judged on keeping the message clear and credible, which response is best?

options.label: Present the first seven slides unchanged and tell investors the rest is in the appendix, which keeps your original order intact.
Drop the least decisive sections, keep one core claim with its strongest evidence and the ask, and rehearse that cut line quickly.
Keep every section and speak faster, so investors still receive the full deck and none of the evidence is dropped.
Skip the opening hook and the closing ask, because the data slides carry the substance and investors value numbers most.

rubric: Cutting to the essential claim, evidence and ask keeps clarity; compressing speed hurts comprehension.
Distractors drop the ask, which is the purpose, or truncate arbitrarily and lose the conclusion.

items.prompt: The rule 'tell them what you will tell them' is standard. In which case does it most clearly work against the speaker's goal?

options.label: A conference session with a printed agenda, where repeating the outline aloud costs a minute but aids those who skipped reading it.
A virtual briefing where attendees join late and need an orientation to follow the remaining sections without confusion.
A persuasive talk to a resistant audience whose force depends on a reveal, so previewing the conclusion invites early counter-arguing.
A 60-minute technical lecture where listeners must hold many parts together and benefit from an early outline of the structure.

rubric: Previewing the conclusion can trigger early rebuttals when persuasion relies on a built-up reveal.
The other cases are those where previews aid orientation, so the rule works there.

items.prompt: A speaker plans to answer every Q&A question with total confidence and never say 'I don't know'. Which are well-founded critiques of this plan? Select all that apply.

options.label: Bridging away from questions to prepared points can read as evasive and erode trust with the questioner.
Confidence comes entirely from vocal volume, so the real weakness is that the speaker has not practised speaking louder.
An invented answer that is later checked costs more credibility than a brief honest limit would have.
Audiences always punish any admission of ignorance, so the plan is correct but should be applied more forcefully.

rubric: Fabrication and evasion both damage trust; a bounded honest answer with follow-up is stronger.
Distractors assume admission is always punished or reduce confidence to volume.

items.prompt: Your microphone dies 15 minutes into a 30-minute talk to 300 people in a hall. Technicians say a fix takes about four minutes. Judged on preserving the message and audience trust, what is the best response?

options.label: Continue at normal volume with your slides, since most of the audience can read the text and the verbal content is secondary.
Stop completely, apologise repeatedly and wait in silence until the equipment returns, to show respect for the audience's time.
Ask the audience to take a ten-minute break at once, which lets you rebuild the talk and avoids any visible struggle.
Say calmly that sound is being fixed, project to the front rows or invite the audience closer, and continue with the core points.

rubric: A calm acknowledgement plus keeping momentum on core points retains trust and message.
Silence, relying on slides, or a long break each waste time or lose the message.

items.prompt: Design a 5-minute talk to a mixed group of engineers and finance managers who must decide on a budget today. Which structure meets all constraints?

options.label: Start with the technical architecture so engineers trust you, then the cost, then the decision, leaving the ask implied.
Start with a long company history for context, then the options, then the cost, then thank the group for its time.
Start with a joke, present five technical benefits in equal depth, and close by asking whether anyone has questions.
Start with the decision and its cost, give one piece of evidence for each audience's main concern, end with a specific ask.

rubric: A decision-first structure with targeted evidence and an explicit ask fits the time and mixed audience.
Distractors bury the decision, leave the ask implied or ignore finance concerns.

items.prompt: In a 30-minute talk listing nine findings, listeners drift around minute 12. You cannot cut findings or extend time. Which redesign best meets these constraints?

options.label: Group the findings into three themes, with signposted transitions, a brief recap after each, and one concrete example per theme.
Move the hardest findings to the end, and promise in the opening that the most important result comes last.
Place all nine findings on one dense slide so the audience sees the whole picture and can read ahead independently.
Speak faster through the findings so the list ends sooner, leaving ten minutes for a longer question session instead.

rubric: Chunking with signposts and examples reduces load without cutting content or time.
Distractors compress, overload visually or merely reorder the same flat list.

items.prompt: A high-stakes 20-minute talk is in three days, and you can rehearse about 90 minutes in total. Which rehearsal plan best uses that time?

options.label: Re-read the slides silently several times each day, since silent review covers all the content in the least time.
Do three full runs on the final evening, because recency makes the material easier to recall during the talk.
Practise the opening twenty times until perfect, and leave the rest unrehearsed so it sounds fresh on the day.
Rehearse aloud in sections, do one timed full run in venue-like conditions, then only light review on the final day.

rubric: Spoken, chunked practice plus a realistic timed run and tapering prepares delivery and timing.
Distractors use silent reading, over-rehearse only the opening, or cram at the end.

items.prompt: A proposed design for a persuasive talk to a sceptical board has a hook, three claims with evidence, a story and a closing ask. The goal is board approval. What is the design most clearly missing?

options.label: A second story, because boards approve on emotion, so more narrative would make up for any weakness in the evidence.
A longer agenda slide, because a detailed roadmap is what makes a board trust the speaker's preparation.
A bigger opening statistic, since the shock value of the first thirty seconds is what decides board approval.
A plan to address the board's most likely objection, so the case does not end up depending on silence about it.

rubric: A sceptical board's likely objection must be handled openly or the case stays vulnerable.
Distractors add more of what is already present or rely on shock, emotion or roadmaps.

items.prompt: Your talk's goal is for listeners to start a new habit within a week. Which closing design best fits this goal?

options.label: Give one concrete first step with a time and place, put it in a short memorable phrase, and ask for a commitment.
Summarise all key points again in order, then thank the audience warmly for their attention and finish on time.
End with a quotation from a famous figure about change, so the audience leaves feeling inspired about the topic.
Offer many options for actions, so each listener can choose what suits them best and feel free to decide later.

rubric: A single specific step with a trigger and a memorable phrase supports behaviour change.
Distractors summarise, inspire vaguely or overload choices, none of which prompts action.

items.prompt: You will give a 15-minute talk, with no interpreter, to an audience where half are non-native English speakers. Which design elements meet this constraint? Select all that apply.

options.label: Read the slide text aloud quickly so listeners hear and see the same words, which saves explanation time.
Pack the slides with jargon, so every listener recognises the field's vocabulary and sees your expertise.
Pair each key term with a simple visual and repeat it consistently rather than using synonyms.
Use short sentences at a slightly slower pace and avoid idioms.

rubric: Plain structure, pacing and consistent terms with visuals aid comprehension.
Jargon and fast reading overload non-native listeners.

items.prompt: You will give the same talk twice: once to 12 people in a meeting room, then to 400 in an auditorium with a stage and a screen. Design the adaptation that best fits both settings.

options.label: Keep the room version conversational and interactive, and in the auditorium use larger gestures, slower pacing, fewer bolder slides and rehearsed questions.
For the auditorium, move quickly among the audience with a handheld microphone and hold open discussion throughout the talk.
Use identical slides, gestures and pacing for both, because consistency means the same practised talk works anywhere.
Shrink the auditorium version to a reading of detailed slides, because large audiences retain written information better than speech.

rubric: Scale changes the delivery: intimacy and interaction in a small room, projection and simplicity in a large one.
Distractors ignore scale, assume impractical open discussion at 400, or replace speaking with reading.
